idiom_name: abstract Expr + concrete node classes with named fields and visitor/instanceof dispatch
implementation_notes: Parr's own implementation of the pattern is a Java class hierarchy: an abstract node base plus concrete classes that hold the named children (AddNode { ExprNode left, right; }) with node-specific methods, and traversal through instanceof tests or a Visitor. The type system enforces field types but neither arity nor dispatch completeness, so constructors validate and exhaustive dispatch stays a convention; keep this form on Java 8-17 or whenever nodes carry behaviour.
pitfalls: instanceof chains and visitors are not checked for completeness: a new node type compiles everywhere and fails at run time with a ClassCastException or a silently skipped branch.
A Visitor needs one visit overload per node type, so every new node type breaks every visitor - the expression problem, which only sealed hierarchies address.

variants.name: Sealed interface with records and pattern switch
variants.idiom_name: sealed interface + record components + exhaustive pattern switch
variants.implementation_notes: Java 21 closes the hierarchy: a sealed interface permits the node records, record components are the named, typed children, and a pattern-matching switch binds them without casts; because the hierarchy is sealed the switch is exhaustive and needs no default. Choose it for new work on Java 21+, and keep the classic class hierarchy when nodes must be mutable or the code must run on older runtimes.
pitfalls: Records are only shallowly immutable: a List<Expr> component can still be mutated, so child lists need wrapping or defensive copies.
Exhaustiveness depends on the sealed hierarchy being visible; adding a permitted subtype later breaks downstream switches at compile time - intended, but a source-breaking change.
